prompt: Which question does verification ask?
hint: Boehm put it in five words.

choices.text: Is this what the people using it need?
choices.why: That is validation: it compares with the need, not the document.

choices.text: Does it match what was specified?
choices.why: Right: are we building it right, against R1 to R9.

choices.text: Has a test run every line of its code?
choices.why: That is a coverage question about the code, and says nothing about the specification.

choices.text: Does the build start and answer at all?
choices.why: That is the smoke question of lesson 8, a much smaller one.

prompt: Ana books two Hamlet tickets as the member and the order says 10% off, R$ 144,00, as R5 gives. What has she done?
hint: What did she compare the order with?

choices.text: Validated the member discount, because she used real data
choices.why: Real data does not change what the result was compared with: a written rule.

choices.text: A static test of R5, since nothing about R5 changed
choices.why: She ran the program; static testing runs nothing.

choices.text: Verified one case of R5
choices.why: Right: a written expectation, a result, and anybody holding R5 could decide it.

choices.text: An acceptance test of the discount rules
choices.why: Acceptance is the client trying it against their own criteria, lesson 12.

prompt: Match each activity to what it compares.
hint: One of them never leaves the paper.

pairs.right: The product with what its users need
The requirements with themselves and each other

right_distractors: The product with its previous release

prompt: Which of these passes verification and fails validation?
hint: One check passes on paper and loses a customer.

choices.text: boxoffice refuses an order of six tickets for Hamlet, although R4 allows one to six per order
choices.why: That fails verification: the product departs from R4.

choices.text: boxoffice refuses a school's thirty tickets, as R4 says, and the school goes elsewhere
choices.why: Right: built as specified, and the specification misses a need.

choices.text: Rui lets paid orders be cancelled, against R6, and the manager likes it
choices.why: The reverse: it fails verification and may pass validation.

choices.text: The home page shows São Paulo times, as R1 says, and customers read them right
choices.why: Both pass: the requirement and the need agree.

prompt: Which properties does a review look for in a requirement? Choose every one that applies.
hint: Four of them; the tester's own question is the last.

choices.text: It has one reading
choices.why: Two careful readers come away with the same rule.

choices.text: It is testable
choices.why: Somebody could decide pass or fail without asking its author.

choices.text: It fits on one line
choices.why: R5 is four sentences and none of its problems is its length.

choices.text: It is consistent with the others
choices.why: R1 and R4 have to agree about what a time means.

choices.text: It was written by the developer
choices.why: Who wrote it is not a property of the sentence; here the manager did.

choices.text: It is complete
choices.why: It says what happens in every case it covers, the awkward ones too.

prompt: Which review finding gives the theatre's manager the most to answer?
hint: Could she reply in one line?

choices.text: R5 is unclear and should be rewritten
choices.why: Unclear how? She has nothing to answer.

choices.text: R5: half per ticket or per order? A member with two student children pays R$ 152,00 or R$ 120,00
choices.why: Right: the id, the two readings and what each costs.

choices.text: R5 is wrong as written: half price has to apply per ticket, as it does at the other theatres in São Paulo
choices.why: That decides the question for its owner, from the tester's own idea.

choices.text: R5 needs more detail about how the discounts work
choices.why: Which detail? It points at the area and asks nothing.

prompt: Read R5 per ticket: Bia, a member, books Hamlet (R$ 80,00) for herself and her two children, who are students. What would the order cost, in reais?
hint: Her ticket gets the member's 10%; each child's gets half. Discounts do not add up.

prompt: boxoffice has one Student box per order. What does that tell you about R5?
hint: Who chose that layout?

choices.text: R5 was clear all along, and boxoffice follows it
choices.why: R5 does not say per order; two readings fit it.

choices.text: It is a defect in boxoffice, to report against R5
choices.why: Against which reading? The product fits one of them.

choices.text: The developer chose one reading of R5, alone
choices.why: Right: an ambiguity left open gets answered by whoever writes the code.

choices.text: A review of R5 needs the running program to find it
choices.why: Reading R5 for its second meaning finds it with nothing running.

prompt: Order these reviews from the least formal to the most formal.
hint: The last one keeps figures.
trap: An inspection is the one with roles and a checklist, so it cannot come first.

prompt: Ana notes that R4 does not say in whose time "one hour before" is counted. What kind of finding is it?
hint: She ran nothing to find it.

choices.text: A defect in boxoffice, to report to Rui
choices.why: Nothing was run, and no reading has been shown wrong yet.

choices.text: A compatibility problem with foreign browsers
choices.why: A browser does not decide when booking closes.

choices.text: A preference of the tester's, to keep to herself
choices.why: It is a gap two people could fill two ways, which is not taste.

choices.text: An ambiguity, for the requirement's owner
choices.why: Right: two readings, and the manager decides which one R4 means.

prompt: Why does a journey show what a requirement-by-requirement pass misses?
hint: The teacher booking her class.

choices.text: It runs more cases in the same amount of time
choices.why: The school journey is one booking; its value is where it starts, not how many.

choices.text: It follows a real customer to what they came for
choices.why: Right: a need no single requirement covers shows up on the way.

choices.text: It checks each requirement more strictly than a case does
choices.why: It checks none more strictly; R4 passes either way.

choices.text: It needs no requirements, so it has no ambiguities
choices.why: It still meets R4; it just asks whether R4 is enough.

prompt: boxoffice answers thirty tickets with "You can book 1 to 6 tickets." Which describes it?
hint: Two requirements apply, and a teacher.

choices.text: It fails R4, since thirty is a valid number of seats
choices.why: R4 sets 1 to 6 per order, so refusing thirty is what R4 asks.

choices.text: It fails R7, because the order was refused
choices.why: R7 asks for a sentence instead of an error page, and this is a sentence.

choices.text: Passes R4 and R7; a question for the owner
choices.why: Right: verified twice, and a validation finding for the owner.

choices.text: It passes both, so there is nothing to tell anybody
choices.why: Passing the requirements says nothing about whether they serve the school.

prompt: Which of these is a finding about the need rather than the tester's taste?
hint: What makes it something to argue with?

choices.text: I would put the price before the date
choices.why: A preference: nothing outside the tester supports it.

choices.text: Modern ticket sites put the price first
choices.why: Borrowed authority, and about other sites' customers.

choices.text: Three of five regulars I watched asked the price
choices.why: Right: evidence of what real customers did, which the owner can weigh.

choices.text: Rui agrees with me that the price should come before the date
choices.why: Two opinions are still opinions; neither is the audience's.

prompt: A validation finding offers readings, not a ___.
hint: The owner gives that.

prompt: Match each finding to where it goes.
hint: One kind of finding goes in the defect tracker.

pairs.left: R4 can be read two ways
pairs.right: A question to the manager before cases are written

pairs.left: boxoffice meets R4 and a school cannot book
pairs.right: The manager, with the school's journey

prompt: Ana files "boxoffice refuses a school group" as a defect. What happens next, most likely?
hint: Rui reads R4.

choices.text: It is closed as working as specified, and the question goes with it
choices.why: Right: correct about the product, and the manager never hears it.

choices.text: Rui raises the limit to thirty, since a defect was filed
choices.why: R4 says six; changing it is the owner's call, not the developer's.

choices.text: The manager reads it in the tracker and decides
choices.why: The section's point is that she does not read the tracker.

choices.text: It becomes a defect against R7 instead
choices.why: R7 is met: the refusal is a sentence.

prompt: Rui made boxoffice depart from R6, and the manager likes the change. What should Ana do?
hint: Think of the next tester who reads R6.

choices.text: Nothing: the person who owns the need is happy
choices.why: R6 still says the old thing, so the next test of R6 reports it again.

choices.text: Rewrite R6 herself to match what boxoffice does
choices.why: Proposing wording is fine; deciding it is the owner's.

choices.text: Report it as a defect and say it looks better
choices.why: Right: one of the two has to change, and the report is how the choice reaches her.

choices.text: Change her cases to expect the new behaviour
choices.why: Then her cases cite a rule nobody wrote.

prompt: The manager answers the R5 question. Put the change in the order the lesson gives.
hint: The written thing moves first.
items: R5 is rewritten with the answer
The cases that cite R5 are updated
The changed cases are run against it
trap: Changing the product first leaves the cases checking it against the old R5.

prompt: R2 allows names of 1 to 40 characters. A customer whose full name has 52 characters cannot sign up with it. What is this finding?
hint: Is R2 unclear, or is boxoffice wrong?

choices.text: A defect against R2, for Rui
choices.why: boxoffice does what R2 says; there is no departure to report.

choices.text: An ambiguity in R2, since 40 has two readings
choices.why: Forty characters has one reading here; the trouble is the number.

choices.text: A validation finding, for the manager
choices.why: Right: the product meets R2 and R2 may miss a real customer.

choices.text: No finding: the customer can type a shorter name
choices.why: Perhaps, and the owner decides that once she knows it happens.

prompt: In the V model, every level of testing checks the product against the document opposite it. Which question can no level on the right side answer from its document alone?
hint: qa-fundamentals lesson 9 draws the V.

choices.text: Whether the code matches its detailed design
choices.why: That is the lowest pair of the V, a verification.

choices.text: Whether the document at the top was right
choices.why: Right: that is validation, and acceptance testing is the level closest to it.

choices.text: Whether the parts work together as the architecture says
choices.why: Integration against architecture is another pair across the V.

choices.text: Whether the whole system meets the system requirements
choices.why: That is system testing against its document, still verification.

prompt: Reviewing R1 to R9 without running boxoffice is ___ testing.
hint: The opposite of dynamic.

prompt: Unsure whether half price is per ticket, Ana writes her cases to expect per ticket and reports boxoffice's per-order total as a defect. What went wrong?
hint: Whose rule is in her expected result?

choices.text: Nothing: per ticket is how theatres charge
choices.why: Maybe, and the manager has not said so; the expected result is Ana's opinion.

choices.text: She filled the gap herself instead of asking its owner
choices.why: Right: test as written, and send the question to the manager.

choices.text: She should have reported it against R7 instead
choices.why: R7 is about error messages, and none is involved.

choices.text: She reported it too early, before running all of R5's cases
choices.why: Running more cases against her own rule would not fix whose rule it is.
